title: American Well Works Co. v. Layne & Bowler Co. (1916)
summary: The state-law business-injury claim did not become a federal patent case merely because patent accusations supplied the disputed statements.
notes:
This is a short assigned note. It supplies no complete lower-court history or full account of the commercial transactions.

American Well Works sued in Arkansas state court for slander of its patented pump; Layne removed, the district court dismissed on the theory that the suit arose under patent law, and the Supreme Court (Holmes, J., with Justice McKenna dissenting) reversed, stating the creation test: a suit arises under the law that creates the cause of action.

sections.Parties: American Well Works asserted that Layne & Bowler had injured its business through statements concerning patent infringement.
sections.Material Facts: The asserted wrong concerned threats or statements damaging the plaintiff’s business. The possible truth of the infringement accusation implicated patent law, but the plaintiff’s requested relief arose from the state-law wrong concerning those statements.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court rejected the federal patent-jurisdiction theory. The casebook uses Justice Holmes’s formulation to introduce the creation test.
sections.Issue: Did a patent question associated with the challenged statements make the plaintiff’s state-law action arise under federal patent law?
sections.Holding: No. The law creating the plaintiff’s cause of action was state law.
sections.Reasoning: The case locates the jurisdictional inquiry in the right asserted by the plaintiff. A federal defense or subsidiary patent controversy is different from a federally created claim. The creation test gives a useful starting rule, while Smith and Grable show that it does not exhaust the exceptional cases in which a state-law claim necessarily presents a substantial federal issue.

learning.why: The state-law business-injury claim did not become a federal patent case merely because patent accusations supplied the disputed statements.

topics.cp-federal-question: The Court described a suit as arising under the law that creates the cause of action.
topics.cp-well-pleaded: A patent issue involved in a defense did not convert the state business-injury claim into a federal claim.
topics.cp-removal: The case reached federal court by removal, and the holding that the claim did not arise under patent law meant removal was improper.
topics.cp-usc-1331: Holmes's creation test is the baseline reading of the 'arising under' language in section 1331.
